title: Numbers, time and dates
objectives: I can count from zero to one hundred and read out a phone number.
I can say how old I am and ask other people's age with 'ter'.
I can ask for and tell the time, including half past, quarter past and on the dot.
I can name the days of the week and the months and say today's date.
I can say when a class, a meeting or a birthday is.
I can explain why the number, time and calendar words are spelled and pronounced the way they are.

vocabulary.note: The 'z' at the start of a word is [z], as in English 'zoo'. The 'e' is open [ɛ] although no accent marks it, so the word is said ZEH-roo. The final 'o' is said 'u'.

Also the indefinite article 'a' or 'an': the number and the article are the same word, so 'um dia' is 'a day' or 'one day'. The 'm' at the end of a word nasalizes the vowel [ũ] and the lips do not close. Feminine: 'uma'.
The 'oi' is a diphthong (one beat), said like the 'oy' of 'boy'. Feminine: 'duas'. The numbers one and two are the only ones below one hundred that change for gender.

A stressed one-syllable word that ends in 'e' plus 's' takes a written accent (lesson on stress and accent marks). The circumflex also shows the closed 'e', as in 'say' without the glide. The 'r' after 't' is a tap. Three does not change for gender.
The 'z' at the end of a word is said 's' in São Paulo and 'sh' in Rio. The 'e' is open although no accent marks it. 'Dez' is also the first part of 'dezesseis', 'dezessete', 'dezoito' and 'dezenove'.
'Qu' before 'i' is said 'k' and the 'u' is silent. The 'n' only nasalizes the 'i' [ˈkĩzi]. The ending '-ze' in 'onze', 'doze', 'treze', 'catorze' and 'quinze' comes from the Latin word for ten.
The 'n' nasalizes the 'i'. A 't' before the sound 'i', which includes a final 'e' (said 'i'), becomes [tʃ], like 'ch' in 'cheese': VEEN-chee.

'C' before 'e' is said 's'. The 'em' at the end of a word is a nasal vowel with a glide, [ẽj̃]. Exactly one hundred is 'cem', and it also stays 'cem' before a noun, as in 'cem anos'. From 101 to 199 the form is 'cento', as in 'cento e um'.
Irregular. Portuguese uses 'ter', not 'ser', to give your age, because you have years. 'Tem' also means 'there is'.
The 'a' is slightly nasal because the 'n' starts the next syllable (a-no). The plural 'anos' means 'years', and a final unstressed 'os' is said 'us'. Also used for age.
Used with 'ter'. 'Quantos' means 'how many' and agrees with 'anos' (masculine plural). 'Qu' before 'a' is [kw], and the 'an' nasalizes the 'a': KWAN-tus.

'C' before 'e' is said 's'. The word ends in 'r', so its default stress is on the last syllable, and no accent is needed. In Portugal people say 'telemóvel'. In the question 'Qual é o seu celular?' the word stands for the phone number.

example.source_literal: The cell phone is of-the Paulo.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable (NÚ-me-ro), which no ending predicts, so the accent is written. On 'u' the acute only marks stress, because Portuguese has just one 'u' sound.

example.target: O número é oito, sete, seis, cinco.
example.source: The number is eight, seven, six, five.

vocabulary.note: The 'h' is silent, a spelling kept from Latin: [ˈɔɾɐ]. The 'o' is open although no accent marks it. In the plural it is used to tell the time: 'São duas horas'.
Unstressed 'que' is said 'ki', and the 'u' after 'q' before 'e' is silent. 'São' is the nasal diphthong 'ão'. The plural 'horas' and 'são' are used even when the answer is one o'clock: 'É uma hora'.

example.source: Excuse me, what time is it?

vocabulary.note: Masculine, because 'dia' is masculine. 'Meio' is an adjective meaning 'half', and it changes to 'meia' before a feminine noun. The 'd' before 'i' is said [dʒ], like 'j' in 'jeans': DJEE-a.
Feminine, because 'noite' is feminine, so the adjective is 'meia'. The 'ei' is a diphthong, and the 't' before the final 'e' (said 'i') is [tʃ]: NOY-chee.
Used after the hour: 'três e meia' is half past three. It is feminine because it stands for 'meia hora', half an hour. The masculine form is 'meio', as in 'meio-dia'.
The 'em' before 'p' is a nasal vowel, and the 'm' only marks the nasal sound; the lips do not close. Used right after the hour: 'duas horas em ponto'.

The 'nh' is the single sound [ɲ], like 'ny' in 'canyon'. The tilde makes the 'a' nasal and also marks the stress, because 'ã' defaults to the last syllable. After a time, 'da manhã' means 'in the morning', from 'de' + 'a' (of the morning), and Brazilians say it instead of 'a.m.'

example.source: It is nine in the morning.

vocabulary.note: The 'd' before the final 'e' (said 'i') is [dʒ]: TAR-dji. The 'r' before a consonant varies by region. 'Da tarde' is used for the hours from noon until about sunset.

example.source: It is three in the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: The 'oi' is a diphthong, and the 't' before the final 'e' is [tʃ]. One word covers both 'night' and 'evening', so 'da noite' is used for the hours after sunset.
The 'au' is a diphthong, like 'ow' in 'cow': OW-la.
Written as one word but related to 'a manhã', the morning. Same spelling logic as 'manhã': 'nh' is one sound and the tilde marks the nasal vowel and the stress.

'Segunda' means 'second' and 'feira' comes from Latin 'feria', a day of the week. The week is counted from Sunday, so Monday is the second day. 'Terça', 'quarta', 'quinta' and 'sexta' continue as 'third', 'fourth', 'fifth' and 'sixth'. Feminine, because 'feira' is. In speech people often say just 'segunda'.
Stressed on the third to last syllable (SÁ-ba-do), so it carries the accent. Masculine and has no '-feira'. The word comes from the Hebrew Sabbath.
The 'in' is a nasal vowel, and the 'g' before 'o' is the hard sound [g]. Masculine and has no '-feira'. The word comes from the Latin for the day of the Lord.

A stressed one-syllable word ending in 'e' plus 's' takes an accent, and the circumflex shows the closed 'e'. In the plural the accent disappears: 'meses' is stressed on the second to last syllable, which is the default for the ending 'es'.
'J' is always [ʒ], like the 's' of 'measure'. The 'ei' is a diphthong: zha-NAY-roo. Months are written with a lower case letter in Portuguese.
The ending 'ão' is a nasal diphthong and defaults to the last syllable, so no accent is needed.
The 'in' is a nasal vowel because the 'n' is followed by a consonant.
A false friend: 'data' means a calendar date, not 'data' in the sense of information, which is 'dados'.

example.target: Qual é a data de hoje?
example.source_literal: Which is the date of today?

vocabulary.note: An ordinal number, meaning a number that gives position in a sequence. It is used for the first day of a month only; every other day uses the ordinary number. The 'ei' is a diphthong, and both 'r' letters are taps.

example.source: Today is the first of May.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the third to last syllable (a-ni-ver-SÁ-rio, the 'io' counting as two beats, as in 'história'), so it carries the accent. Literally the same word as 'anniversary', and it also means any yearly anniversary.
'Qu' before 'a' is [kw], and the 'an' before 'd' is nasal: KWAN-du.
Portuguese has no word for the 'it' of 'it is'. The verb 'é' has no subject word. The 'h' of 'hoje' is silent and the 'j' is [ʒ]: OH-zhee. Answers with a weekday or with a date.

grammar.title: Cardinal numbers from 0 to 100
grammar.explanation:
A cardinal number is a number used for counting ('one', 'two', 'three'). An ordinal number gives a position in a sequence ('first', 'second', 'third'). This note covers cardinals. Portuguese counts in tens, like English, and the system has three layers. Once you see the layers, you only have to memorize the first one.

Layer one is the irregular words from zero to fifteen. They are old forms with no pattern, so you learn them one by one: 'zero', 'um', 'dois', 'três', 'quatro', 'cinco', 'seis', 'sete', 'oito', 'nove', 'dez', 'onze', 'doze', 'treze', 'catorze', 'quinze'. The five words from 'onze' to 'quinze' all end in '-ze', a shortened form of the Latin word for ten. 'Catorze' is also written 'quatorze', and both are correct.

Layer two is sixteen to nineteen, which are transparent: ten plus the unit, fused into one written word. 'Dezesseis' is 'dez e seis', 'ten and six'; 'dezessete' is 'ten and seven'; 'dezoito' is 'ten and eight'; 'dezenove' is 'ten and nine'. Portugal writes 'dezasseis' and 'dezassete', but Brazil writes 'dezesseis' and 'dezessete'. The spelling note after this one explains the double 's'.

Layer three is the tens: 'vinte', 'trinta', 'quarenta', 'cinquenta', 'sessenta', 'setenta', 'oitenta', 'noventa'. The ending '-nta' in the last seven comes from a Latin ending that meant tens. To build a number between the tens, put the word 'e' (and) between the tens and the unit: 'vinte e um', 'trinta e cinco', 'noventa e nove'. English joins these with a hyphen ('twenty-one') and Portuguese writes them as three separate words with 'e'. The number one hundred is 'cem' when nothing follows it (and before a noun: 'cem anos') and 'cento' when more follows: 'cento e um', one hundred and one.

Only 'um' and 'dois' have a feminine form: 'uma' and 'duas'. They must agree with the noun that follows, which means they take the gender of that noun. So it is 'um ano' (masculine) but 'uma hora' (feminine), 'dois meses' but 'duas horas'. The agreement also reaches inside compound numbers: 'vinte e um anos', 'vinte e uma horas', 'trinta e dois anos', 'trinta e duas horas'. Among the numbers up to one hundred, three and above never change. Remember also that 'um' is both the number one and the indefinite article 'a' or 'an': 'um dia' means 'a day' or 'one day', and the context decides.

To read a phone number, say the digits one at a time. In Brazil the first two digits are the area code, called DDD, and 11 is São Paulo. Many people say 'meia', short for 'meia dúzia', half a dozen ('dúzia' is stressed on its first syllable, the third to last when the final 'ia' counts as two beats, so it carries an accent), in place of 'seis' when reading a number aloud, because 'seis' can be mistaken for other digits on a bad line.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why the number words are written as they are
grammar.explanation:
Every number word is built from rules you already have. This note applies them, so that you can read the numbers aloud and understand why each is spelled as it is. The rules are the ones from the lessons on sounds, on stress and accent marks, and on how Portuguese works. Brackets show the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet, a system with one symbol per sound.

Four rules explain most of the table. First, 'c' and 'qu' depend on the vowel after them. Before 'e' or 'i', 'c' is [s]; before 'a', 'o' or 'u' it is [k]. So the first 'c' of 'cinco' is [s] and the second is [k]. 'Qu' before 'e' or 'i' is [k] with a silent 'u' ('quinze'), and 'qu' before 'a' is [kw] ('quatro', 'quarenta'). Second, a nasal vowel is written with 'm' or 'n' before a consonant, or with 'm' at the end of a word. The letter only tells you to send air through the nose; it is not a separate consonant. That is why 'um', 'cinco', 'onze', 'quinze', 'vinte' and 'trinta' are nasal, and why 'cem' ends in a nasal vowel with a glide. Third, a 't' before the sound 'i', which includes a final 'e' (said 'i'), becomes [tʃ], like 'ch' in 'cheese': 'sete' is SEH-chee and 'vinte' is VEEN-chee. A 't' before any other sound is plain: 'oito', 'trinta', 'setenta'. Fourth, between two vowels a single 's' or 'z' is [z], so Portuguese doubles the 's' to write the sound [s] there. 'Dezesseis' and 'dezessete' have 'ss' for that reason; with a single 's' they would be said with [z]. The 'z' of 'dezoito' and 'dezenove' is simply [z], as the rule predicts.

Accents appear only where the stress rule is broken. 'Três' is a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'e' plus 's', so it takes an accent, and the circumflex also shows that the 'e' is closed. 'Cinquenta' is an exception to the rule about 'qu': the 'u' after 'q' before 'e' is pronounced, [sĩˈkwẽtɐ], like 'tranquilo' and 'linguiça' in the lesson on sounds. Learn it as a single word. Finally, 'e' (and) has no accent and is said [i], while 'é' (is) has an acute because it is a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'e', and it is said [ɛ].

No other number word carries a written accent, because every other number is stressed where its ending predicts. Whether an 'e' or 'o' with no mark is open or closed ('sete', 'nove', 'zero' and 'dez' are open; 'doze' and 'treze' are closed) must be learned with the word, as the lesson on sounds said.

grammar.title: Ter in the present, and saying your age
grammar.explanation:
'Ter' means 'to have'. A verb form is the shape a verb takes for one person, and 'ter' is irregular, which means its forms do not follow the regular pattern for verbs in '-er' and must be learned one by one. The present is: 'eu tenho', 'você tem', 'ele tem' and 'ela tem', 'nós temos', 'a gente tem', 'vocês têm', 'eles têm' and 'elas têm'. A regular '-er' verb would give a form like 'teno' for 'eu'; the irregular form is 'tenho', with 'nh', the single sound [ɲ] of 'canyon'. As usual, 'você', 'ele', 'ela' and 'a gente' share one form, and 'vocês', 'eles' and 'elas' share another.

The accent in 'têm' needs a reason, because the stress rule does not demand it. 'Tem' and 'têm' are both a single stressed syllable and sound exactly the same in Brazilian Portuguese: [tẽj̃]. The circumflex is a differential accent, a mark added only in writing, so that the reader can tell 'he has' ('tem') from 'they have' ('têm'). It does not show a closed vowel here, and it is not the same use as in 'você'.

Portuguese gives age with 'ter', not with 'ser'. English treats age as a state you are in ('I am thirty'); Portuguese treats years as something you possess: 'Eu tenho trinta anos', literally 'I have thirty years'. The question is 'Quantos anos você tem?', literally 'how many years you have'. 'Quantos' means 'how many' and agrees with 'anos' (masculine plural), the same agreement as 'um' in 'vinte e um anos'. The word 'anos' is always included in a full sentence; in conversation the short answer 'Trinta' is possible.

Questions are made with intonation, as in all yes or no questions: 'Você tem vinte anos?' To negate, put 'não' before the verb: 'Eu não tenho trinta anos', literally 'I not have thirty years'. 'Ter' is used for other things you own or carry ('Tenho um celular') and, in Brazilian speech, for 'there is': 'Tem café' means 'there is coffee'.

grammar.title: Small words in the dialogues: qual, meu and seu, né
grammar.explanation:
'Qual' is a question word, like 'quem', 'como', 'onde' and 'o que' from the earlier lessons. It means 'which', and it asks you to pick one item from a set. Where English asks 'What is your phone number?', Portuguese asks 'Qual é o seu celular?', literally 'Which is the your cell phone'. English 'what' and Portuguese 'qual' do not map one to one: to ask what a thing is, Portuguese uses 'o que' ('O que é isso?'), and to ask for one particular item, such as a number, a date or a name, it uses 'qual'. The plural is 'quais': 'Quais são os números?'

'Meu' and 'seu' are possessives, words that say whose something is. 'Meu' is 'my' and 'seu' is 'your' when you are speaking to 'você'. A possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner: 'meu celular', but 'minha casa'. Brazilians often put the article before it ('o meu aniversário', 'o seu celular'), and before a noun it is optional ('meu aniversário' is also correct). The article plus the possessive can also stand alone for a noun already mentioned: 'O meu é onze, nove, oito' means 'Mine is eleven, nine, eight'. A later lesson explains possessives fully; here you only need 'meu', 'o meu' and 'o seu'.

'Né' is a spoken, informal contraction of 'não é', literally 'not is', put at the end of a statement to ask for agreement, like English 'right?' or 'isn't it?': 'A aula é às dez, né?' It is said [nɛ], with the open 'e' of 'é', and it is written with an acute for the same reason as 'é': a stressed one-syllable word that ends in 'e' takes an accent. A yes answer to a question with 'é' often repeats the verb: 'É, sim', literally 'is, yes'. 'Desculpa, como?' asks someone to repeat what they said: 'como' here is 'how' or 'what', so the literal sense is 'Sorry, how?' Finally, 'Até amanhã', literally 'Until tomorrow', is a fixed farewell; 'até' means 'until', and it carries an acute because it ends in 'e' but is stressed on the last syllable, breaking the default for that ending, like 'você'.

Also in the dialogues, each spelled by rules you already have. 'Então' (so, then) has the nasal diphthong 'ão', and the 'en' before 't' is nasal. 'Também' (also, too) ends in 'em', and words ending in 'em' are stressed on the second to last syllable by default, so a stress on the last syllable needs the acute accent: tam-BÉM, with the 'em' nasal. 'Tchau' (bye) is written 'tch-au' because 'tch' is a loan spelling for the sound [tʃ], as in 'cheese', and 'au' is a diphthong like 'ow' in 'cow'. 'Isso' (that) has 'ss' between vowels, which writes [s]; a single 's' there would be [z]. 'Ótimo' (great) is stressed on the third to last syllable, so it carries the accent, and the 't' before 'i' is [tʃ]. 'Lindo' (lovely) has a nasal 'in'. 'Legal' (cool) ends in 'l', which is said [w], and the stress is on the last syllable by default. 'Hoje' (today) has a silent 'h' and a 'j' that is [ʒ].

grammar.title: Telling the time
grammar.explanation:
English says 'It is ten o'clock', using the empty word 'it' as a subject. Portuguese has no such word. The subject of the sentence is the hours themselves, and the verb 'ser' agrees with it: 'São dez horas' is literally 'Are ten hours', and the plural verb 'são' is used because 'horas' is plural. For one o'clock the hour is singular, so the verb is singular too: 'É uma hora', 'Is one hour'. Noon and midnight are singular: 'É meio-dia', 'É meia-noite'. The question follows the same logic, 'Que horas são?', literally 'What hours are?', and it is normally plural, even if the answer is 'É uma hora'.

Minutes are added with 'e' (and): 'São três e dez' is ten past three and 'São três e quinze' is quarter past three. To say minutes before the hour, Brazilians most often say 'São dez para as três', literally 'Are ten to the three', meaning ten to three, or 'Faltam dez para as três', literally 'Lack ten to the three'. The form 'São três menos dez', literally 'Are three minus ten', is understood but less common in Brazil. Half past is 'e meia', literally 'and half'. 'Meia' is an adjective, a word that describes a noun, and it takes the feminine form because it stands for 'meia hora', half an hour. The same adjective gives 'meio-dia' (half-day, masculine, because 'dia' is) and 'meia-noite' (half-night, feminine, because 'noite' is). For exactly on the hour say 'em ponto', literally 'in point'.

To say which part of the day, add 'da manhã', 'da tarde' or 'da noite' after the time: 'São oito da manhã'. 'Da' is 'de' + 'a', so 'São três da tarde' is literally 'Are three of-the afternoon'. Brazilians use this instead of 'a.m.' and 'p.m.' The 24 hour clock is used in schedules and announcements: 'quatorze horas' is two in the afternoon.

To say that something happens at a certain time, use the preposition 'a' (at) joined with the article. The article agrees with the hour, which is understood but not said: 'A aula é às nove' means 'The class is at-the nine', because 'horas' is understood, so 'a' + 'as' makes 'às'. For one o'clock the hour is singular and feminine, so 'a' + 'a' makes 'à uma'. Noon is masculine, so 'a' + 'o' makes 'ao meio-dia'. Midnight is feminine, so 'à meia-noite'. The grave accent in 'à' and 'às' only records the fusion of two 'a' sounds, as explained in the lesson on accent marks. In the question 'A que horas é a aula?' (At what time is the class?), there is no article after 'a', so nothing fuses and no accent is written.

grammar.title: Days, months and dates
grammar.explanation:
The names of the weekdays follow a logic. Monday to Friday are numbered, counting from Sunday as the first day: 'segunda-feira' is second, 'terça-feira' third, 'quarta-feira' fourth, 'quinta-feira' fifth, 'sexta-feira' sixth. 'Feira' comes from the Latin 'feria', a day of the week in the church calendar; the same word today also means a market or fair. Saturday and Sunday are not numbered: 'sábado' comes from the Hebrew Sabbath and 'domingo' from the Latin for the day of the Lord. In speech the '-feira' is often dropped ('segunda', 'terça', 'quarta').

Gender follows the noun. The numbered days are feminine because 'feira' is: 'a segunda-feira'. 'Sábado' and 'domingo' are masculine: 'o sábado', 'o domingo'. English says 'on Monday'; Portuguese uses 'em' (in, on, at), which fuses with the article: 'em' + 'a' = 'na', 'em' + 'o' = 'no'. So 'na segunda-feira' and 'no sábado'. Days and months are not capitalized in Portuguese. English capitalizes them as if they were names, and Portuguese treats them as ordinary words.

The months are 'janeiro', 'fevereiro', 'março', 'abril', 'maio', 'junho', 'julho', 'agosto', 'setembro', 'outubro', 'novembro' and 'dezembro'. To say 'in' a month, use 'em' with no article: 'em março', 'em dezembro'. The seasons are 'o verão', 'o outono', 'o inverno' and 'a primavera'. Brazil is in the southern hemisphere, so they run opposite to Europe and North America: summer is roughly December to March and winter June to September.

A date is said day, month, year, joined by 'de' (of): 'dia cinco de maio' is literally 'day five of May'. English uses ordinals ('the fifth of May'); Portuguese uses the ordinary number for every day except the first, which is 'primeiro': 'primeiro de maio'. 'Primeiro' is masculine because 'dia' is understood. The word 'dia' is optional: 'Hoje é cinco de maio' is also correct. To ask, say 'Que dia é hoje?' (the day of the week or the date) or 'Qual é a data de hoje?' (the date).

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why the time and calendar words are written as they are
grammar.explanation:
The time and calendar words use the same few rules as the numbers, plus the accent rules. Three questions explain almost every word. Where is the stress? If the word breaks the default for its ending, there is an accent. Which sounds change with their neighbors? A 't' or 'd' before the sound 'i' becomes [tʃ] or [dʒ]; an 'n' or 'm' after a vowel and before a consonant nasalizes the vowel; 'nh', 'lh' and 'ch' are single sounds. And which letters are silent? 'H' is always silent, and 'u' is silent in 'que', 'qui', 'gue' and 'gui'.

Accents here have three sources. Words stressed on the third to last syllable always take one: 'sábado', 'número', 'aniversário' (the 'io' counts as two beats, as in 'história'), 'ótimo'. Stressed one-syllable words ending in 'e', with or without 's', take one: 'mês', and also 'é', as in 'É uma hora'. And the tilde in 'manhã', 'amanhã' and 'verão' marks the nasal vowel and, with no other accent, also the stress. The accent on 'mês' disappears in 'meses', because that form is stressed on the second to last syllable, the default for the ending 'es', and the 's' between vowels becomes [z].

The grave accent in 'à' and 'às' is a special case: it does not mark stress or sound at all. It only records that the preposition 'a' and the article 'a' or 'as' have fused into one 'a', as explained in the lesson on accent marks.

Month names are a good test of the rules. 'Janeiro': 'j' is always [ʒ]. 'Março': 'ç' before 'o' is [s]. 'Abril': 'l' at the end of a syllable is [w], and the stress falls on the last syllable by default. 'Junho' and 'julho' contain the single sounds [ɲ] and [ʎ]. In 'setembro', 'novembro' and 'dezembro' the 'm' before 'b' is nasal, and in 'setembro' the 't' before a nasal 'e' is plain, because [tʃ] happens only before the sound 'i'. The days follow suit: 'sexta' has 'x' before a consonant, which is [s]; 'quarta' has [kw] and 'quinta' has a silent 'u'; 'terça' has a 'ç'.

culture.title: Time, dates and phone numbers in Brazil
culture.text:
Brazilians write dates in the order day, month, year, so 03/04 is the third of April, not the fourth of March. Months and days are written in lower case. In everyday conversation time is usually said on the 12 hour clock with 'da manhã', 'da tarde' or 'da noite', but train timetables, flight information, TV listings and many official notices use the 24 hour clock: 'dezenove horas' means seven in the evening.

Punctuality is flexible in social situations. A party that starts at 'oito horas' often fills up an hour or two later, and the expression 'hora brasileira', literally 'Brazilian time', jokingly describes this. At work, in class and for medical appointments you are expected to be on time, and 'em ponto' means exactly that. Brazil abolished daylight saving time in 2019, so the clocks no longer change.

Phone numbers have a two digit area code, the DDD, followed by nine digits for cell phones, which always start with 9. Most people use WhatsApp to message, so asking 'Qual é o seu WhatsApp?' is as common as asking for a phone number. The seasons are reversed relative to the northern hemisphere: Christmas in dezembro and New Year come in the middle of the summer, and Carnaval falls in February or early March, at the end of the hot season.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'três' carry an accent mark?
choices: It is stressed on the third to last syllable
It is a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'e' plus 's', and the circumflex shows a closed 'e'
exercises.explanation: A stressed one-syllable word that ends in 'e' plus 's' takes an accent. The circumflex (not the acute) shows that the 'e' is closed. A nasal vowel would need a tilde, or an 'm' or 'n'.

exercises.prompt: How is the first 'c' of 'cinco' pronounced?
exercises.explanation: 'C' before 'e' or 'i' is [s]. The second 'c' of 'cinco' is before 'o', so it is [k].

choices: Between two vowels a single 's' would be said 'z', so 'ss' writes the 's' sound
exercises.explanation: 'Dezesseis' is 'dez' + 'e' + 'seis'. Between vowels a single 's' is [z], and 'ss' is the way to write [s] there.

exercises.prompt: In 'cinquenta', the 'u' after 'q' is pronounced (sin-KWEN-ta), although 'qu' before 'e' is normally 'k' with a silent 'u'. What is the best description?
choices: Numbers follow a different spelling rule
The 'n' turns the 'u' into a glide automatically
The word is a misspelling of 'cincoenta'
It is one of a few words where the 'u' is pronounced, so it is learned word by word
exercises.explanation: 'Cinquenta', 'tranquilo', 'linguiça' and 'aguentar' are words in which the 'u' is pronounced even before 'e' or 'i'.

exercises.prompt: Why is the verb plural in 'São duas horas' but singular in 'É uma hora'?
choices: The subject is the hours, and the verb agrees with it in number
'São' is used in the morning and 'é' in the afternoon
Portuguese has no rule for this
exercises.explanation: Portuguese has no empty subject 'it'. The hours are the subject: 'Are two hours', 'Is one hour'.

exercises.prompt: Which is correct for 'at one o'clock'?
exercises.explanation: 'Hora' is singular and feminine, so 'a' + 'a' fuses into 'à'. 'Às' would need the plural 'horas', and 'ao' would need a masculine word.

exercises.prompt: 'A aula é ao meio-dia' uses 'ao', not 'à'. Why?
choices: 'Meio-dia' is masculine, so the preposition 'a' fuses with the article 'o'
It is an exception with no reason
exercises.explanation: 'Meio-dia' is masculine because 'dia' is. 'A' + 'o' makes 'ao'. Midnight, 'meia-noite', is feminine, so it is 'à meia-noite'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'têm' (they have) carry a circumflex while 'tem' (he has) does not?
choices: 'Têm' is stressed on a different syllable
It is only a written device to tell plural from singular; both sound the same
exercises.explanation: Both are pronounced [tẽj̃] in Brazil. The circumflex is a differential accent that exists only in writing.

exercises.prompt: 'Quinta-feira' is built on 'quinta', meaning 'fifth'. If Sunday is counted as the first day, which day is it?
exercises.explanation: Sunday is first, Monday second, Tuesday third, Wednesday fourth, Thursday fifth.

exercises.prompt: Why is the accent written in 'mês' but not in 'meses'?
choices: 'Mês' is a stressed one-syllable word ending in 'e' plus 's'; 'meses' is stressed on the second to last syllable, which is the default for 'es'
The plural never has an accent
The accent moved to the first 'e'
exercises.explanation: The accent belongs to one form of the word. The longer form follows the default for its ending, so no accent is needed.

exercises.prompt: In 'A aula é às dez, né?', what does 'né' do?
choices: It is short for 'não é' and asks for agreement, like 'right?'
exercises.explanation: 'Né' is an informal spoken contraction of 'não é'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'também' carry an acute accent?
choices: Words ending in 'em' are stressed on the second to last syllable by default, and this one is stressed on the last
The accent shows that the 'e' is closed
It is a one-syllable word ending in 'e' plus 's'
The accent marks the start of a nasal diphthong
exercises.explanation: The default for the ending 'em' is the second to last syllable. Stress on the last syllable breaks that default, so the acute is written. The 'm' only nasalizes the vowel.
Age uses 'ter', not 'ser': literally 'I have thirty years'. The 'eu' form of 'ter' is 'tenho'.

choices: Between two vowels a single 's' would be said 'z', so 'ss' writes the 's' sound
exercises.explanation: The same rule as 'dezesseis': between vowels 's' is [z], and 'ss' is the way to write [s] there.
The plural 'têm' has a circumflex in writing to tell it from the singular 'tem'.
'Um' agrees with the noun that follows, even inside a compound number. 'Anos' is masculine, so 'vinte e um'.
'Horas' is feminine, so the final one is 'uma': 'vinte e uma horas'.
The hours ('horas') are understood and plural, so 'a' + 'as' makes 'às'.
'Sábado' is masculine, and 'em' + 'o' makes 'no'.
A month takes 'em' with no article.

exercises.hint_source: Today is the first of May.
exercises.explanation: The first of the month is the only day said with an ordinal number.
'Meia-noite' is feminine singular, so the preposition 'a' fuses with the article 'a'. The grave accent records the fusion.

answers: Eu tenho vinte e cinco anos.
exercises.explanation: Age uses 'ter' plus 'anos'. Literally: 'I have twenty-five years'.
The question always uses the plural 'horas são'.
Plural verb for three hours, then 'e meia'.
The '-feira' is often dropped in everyday speech.
